Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Fans of Michael Jackson lined the streets outside Harlem's Apollo Theater on Tuesday for a chance to pay their respects to the late "King of Pop" at the hall that helped launch his career. A hat and glittery glove represent Michael Jackson at the Apollo Theater tribute. The crowd stood eight to 10 abreast in the sun and 80-degree weather for 10 blocks, waiting for hours for a chance to enter the theater. Fans were allowed in 600 at a time, where they lay flowers and other mementos at the foot of the stage and danced to Jackson's music as it played over the sound system. "We left our house at 4 o'clock in the morning and got here at 9, and we were lucky to get here," said Angela Staples, who came to New York from Pennsylvania with her daughter Jasmine. "I'm so happy about the outpouring of love and the crowd and the people. It's so respectful to Michael." Those in the hall observed a moment of silence at 5:26 p.m. -- the time Jackson was pronounced dead Thursday in Los Angeles, California. The cause of the 50-year-old singer's death has not yet been determined. An autopsy on the 50-year-old singer was was inconclusive, leaving authorities waiting on the results of toxicology tests to determine what killed him. Fans have been gathering outside the theater since last week to remember Jackson, who at age 9 won a 1967 Apollo amateur night showcase with his brothers in the group the Jackson 5. "While he went on from the Apollo stage to achieve international fame on an unprecedented level, to us and all of you, he's family because he started out here," said Jonelle Procope, the legendary venue's CEO. Jackson became an idol of both black and white fans and was among the first African-American artists to get widespread play on the music-video channel MTV. But in later years, he was known more for a roller-coaster personal life, including extensive plastic surgery, financial woes and a 1995 trial and acquittal on child-molestation charges. The Rev. Al Sharpton, the New York civil rights activist who became a friend of the Jackson family, urged Jackson's fans not to let critics "scandalize" a groundbreaking performer. "Michael wasn't no freak," Sharpton said. "Michael was a genius. Michael was an innovator. You can't take someone with extraordinary skills, extraordinary talent, and make him an ordinary person. He was extraordinary. He lived extraordinarily, and we love him with an extraordinary passion." The Apollo had been one of the top venues for jazz, gospel and soul artists for decades before the Jacksons' breakthrough.  Sharpton said the theater was home to "the best and the baddest." "You've got to come from the stage of the Apollo and go all over the world to understand Michael," Sharpton said. "We understand his journey, because we were with him every step of the way." The Jackson brothers' amateur night win led to a $1,000 deal for 31 shows at the Apollo, said Bobby Schiffman, whose family owned the theater. "Shortly after their appearance, Diana Ross took them on an NBC special that she did, and there was no looking back after that. They just skyrocketed," Schiffman said. Jackson at the time "was a sweet little boy," he said. "He was extremely talented, extremely easy to get along with," Schiffman said. "He always had a smile on his face, and it was a pleasure to see him working in the theater." CNN's Aspen Steib contributed to this report.

Inside the theater, Jackson was symbolized by a hat and a sparkling glove. Outside, people waited for hours in sunny, 80-degree weather. The line stretched for 10 blocks, with fans standing eight to 10 across.

Groups of 600 were admitted at a time. Once inside, mourners placed flowers and other keepsakes near the stage and danced as Jackson’s songs played through the theater’s sound system.

Angela Staples traveled from Pennsylvania with her daughter, Jasmine. She said they had left home at 4 a.m. and reached New York at 9 a.m., adding that they felt fortunate to have made it.

Staples said she was delighted by the size of the crowd and the affection people were showing, describing the tribute as deeply respectful of Jackson.

At 5:26 p.m., everyone inside paused for a moment of silence. That was the time Jackson had been declared dead the previous Thursday in Los Angeles, California.

Officials had not determined what caused the 50-year-old singer’s death. An autopsy produced no conclusive answer, so authorities were awaiting toxicology results.

People had been coming to the Apollo since the previous week to commemorate Jackson. His connection to the theater began in 1967, when, at age 9, he and his brothers won an Apollo amateur-night competition as the Jackson 5.

Apollo CEO Jonelle Procope said that although Jackson went from the theater’s stage to an unmatched degree of worldwide stardom, the Apollo community still regarded him as family because his career began there.

Jackson attracted devoted audiences across racial lines and became one of the earliest African-American performers to receive broad exposure on MTV. In his later life, however, public attention increasingly focused on his turbulent personal affairs, including numerous plastic surgeries, money problems, and his 1995 trial and acquittal on child-molestation allegations.

The Rev. Al Sharpton, a New York civil rights leader and friend of Jackson’s family, called on supporters not to allow detractors to tarnish the reputation of the pioneering entertainer.

Sharpton rejected descriptions of Jackson as a “freak,” instead calling him a brilliant innovator. He said a person with such exceptional gifts and talent could not be treated as ordinary, adding that Jackson lived an extraordinary life and inspired extraordinary love.

Long before the Jackson family’s breakthrough, the Apollo had spent decades as a premier destination for jazz, gospel and soul performers. Sharpton described it as the place where “the best and the baddest” performed.

He said understanding Jackson required recognizing the path from the Apollo stage to worldwide success. According to Sharpton, the Apollo community understood that journey because it had accompanied him throughout it.

Bobby Schiffman, whose family owned the venue, said the Jackson brothers’ amateur-night victory resulted in a $1,000 contract to perform 31 Apollo shows.

Not long after that appearance, Diana Ross featured the group on an NBC television special, Schiffman said. From that point forward, he added, their career took off rapidly.

Schiffman remembered Jackson at that age as a kind young boy who was exceptionally gifted and easy to work with. He said Jackson was always smiling and that watching him perform at the theater was a pleasure.

CNN’s Aspen Steib contributed to this report.

The crowd stretched along 125th Street as Jackson’s music played from car stereos and portable speakers. Some fans wore white gloves, black fedoras and military-style jackets, while others carried photographs, flowers and handwritten signs.

The Apollo marquee read: **“In Memory of Michael Jackson, A True Apollo Legend, 1958–2009.”**

Nearby, fans formed a circle and attempted Jackson’s signature moonwalk. The mood moved between celebration and grief: Crowds cheered when songs such as “Billie Jean” and “Don’t Stop ’Til You Get Enough” began playing, then fell quiet as people placed candles and bouquets near the theater entrance.

“I came here because this is where it started for him,” another attendee said. “The best way to remember Michael is through the music and the dancing.”

The Rev. Al Sharpton addressed the crowd, describing Jackson as a groundbreaking Black entertainer whose influence extended far beyond the stage.

“Michael made culture accept a person of color way before Tiger Woods, way before Oprah Winfrey, way before Barack Obama,” Sharpton said. He called Jackson’s rise from the Apollo stage to worldwide fame a historic achievement.

Sharpton also urged fans to focus on Jackson’s artistic legacy rather than the controversies that followed him later in life.

# From Amateur Night to Memorial: Michael Jackson’s Enduring Bond With the Apollo Theater

When Michael Jackson died on June 25, 2009, the Apollo Theater became one of the most fitting places for the public to mourn him. Fans gathered outside the Harlem landmark, leaving flowers, photographs and handwritten messages beneath a marquee honoring the singer. On June 30, the theater hosted a public tribute that brought thousands of admirers to 125th Street for music, dancing and remembrance.

The setting reflected more than Jackson’s worldwide fame. Decades earlier, the Apollo had helped introduce him as a remarkably gifted child performer.

## An Early Triumph With the Jackson 5

In 1967, Michael and his brothers appeared at the Apollo’s famously demanding Amateur Night as the Jackson 5. The young group won the competition, impressing an audience known for quickly rejecting performers who failed to command the stage.

Michael, still a child, was already the group’s focal point. His assured singing, rhythmic precision and ability to connect with a crowd suggested the qualities that would later define his career. The victory became an important milestone as the brothers moved from local performances in and around Gary, Indiana, toward national recognition.

Soon afterward, the Jackson 5 signed with Motown. Beginning with “I Want You Back,” the group sent its first four major-label singles to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100—a run that also included “ABC,” “The Love You Save” and “I’ll Be There.” Michael’s soaring voice and charismatic performances made him one of the era’s most recognizable young stars.

## Harlem Remembers

By the time mourners assembled at the Apollo in 2009, Jackson’s career had expanded far beyond his beginnings in a family act. The theater opened its doors for a celebration of his life, with fans filing through to hear his music, watch performances and share memories. Outside, the gathering took on the character of a street festival and vigil at once: people sang, imitated Jackson’s dance moves and remembered the moments his work had accompanied in their own lives.

The Apollo’s tribute linked the superstar of *Thriller* to the child who had once faced the theater’s Amateur Night audience. It also placed Jackson within a wider lineage of Black American performers associated with the venue, including Ella Fitzgerald, James Brown, Billie Holiday and countless others whose careers were nurtured or celebrated there.

## A Transformative Cultural Legacy

Jackson’s influence reached across music, dance, fashion and visual media. Albums such as *Off the Wall*, *Thriller* and *Bad* combined pop, R&B, funk, rock and disco with unusually ambitious production. *Thriller* became the best-selling album in history by widely cited measures, while its title film helped transform the music video into a major cinematic and promotional form.

His performances established a new standard for global pop spectacle. The moonwalk—although developed by earlier dancers—became inseparable from Jackson after his 1983 performance of “Billie Jean” on the television special *Motown 25*. His sharp isolations, spins, toe stands and synchronized choreography have been echoed by generations of artists.

Jackson also played a significant role in broadening the visibility of Black performers on mainstream music television. The enormous popularity of videos such as “Billie Jean,” “Beat It” and “Thriller” helped challenge barriers in an industry that had often limited access and exposure.

His legacy remains complicated. Later life brought intense tabloid scrutiny, changing public perceptions and allegations of child sexual abuse, which Jackson denied. He was acquitted of criminal charges in 2005, while debate over the allegations and how they should affect interpretations of his work has continued after his death.

Even amid that complexity, Jackson’s artistic impact is unmistakable. His recordings remain widely heard, his choreography is continually studied and recreated, and his approach to the pop album, music video and stadium performance still shapes contemporary entertainment.

The Apollo memorial captured that enduring reach. It was both a farewell to a global celebrity and a return, in public memory, to one of his earliest proving grounds—the stage where Michael Jackson and the Jackson 5 first showed a famously exacting audience what they could become.

**June 30, 2009 — New York**

**HARLEM, N.Y.** — A line of mourners stretched for roughly 10 blocks outside the Apollo Theater on Tuesday as thousands of fans gathered to celebrate Michael Jackson, five days after the pop superstar’s sudden death in Los Angeles.

The crowd wound along 125th Street and through surrounding blocks, filling the neighborhood with Jackson’s music, handmade signs and impromptu dancing. Some fans wore single sequined gloves; others carried photographs, flowers and posters bearing messages such as “Thank You, Michael” and “Forever the King of Pop.”

The Apollo’s marquee read: **“In Memory of Michael Jackson, A True Apollo Legend, 1958–2009.”**

The theater opened its doors for a public tribute, admitting groups of mourners throughout the day. Inside, fans danced in the aisles and sang along to recordings spanning Jackson’s career, from the Jackson 5’s “I Want You Back” to solo hits including “Billie Jean,” “Beat It” and “Man in the Mirror.” A wall and condolence book allowed visitors to leave personal messages for Jackson’s family.

Jonelle Procope, president and chief executive of the Apollo Theater Foundation, said the response reflected the public’s desire for a place to grieve together. In the days after Jackson’s death, she said, the theater was inundated with calls asking how the Apollo would honor an entertainer whose history was closely tied to the Harlem landmark.

“This is where it all began for Michael Jackson and the Jackson 5,” Procope told reporters, describing the gathering as both a memorial and a celebration of his artistic legacy. She said the Apollo wanted fans to have an opportunity to remember Jackson in the same building where New York audiences first embraced him as a child performer.

Jackson’s connection to the Apollo dates to 1967, when the Jackson 5 competed in the theater’s famously unforgiving Amateur Night. The young group won its competition and soon attracted wider attention, helping set in motion a career that would transform popular music.

Bobby Schiffman, whose family operated the Apollo during that period, recalled the Jackson 5’s early appearance and the impact of the group’s remarkably young lead singer. Jackson, though still a child, performed with confidence and polish beyond his years, Schiffman said. The audience’s reaction made clear that the group—and Michael in particular—possessed unusual star power.

Schiffman described the performance as one of the historic moments that helped define the Apollo’s role as a proving ground for Black artists. The theater’s Amateur Night crowds were known for quickly rejecting performers they disliked, making the Jackson 5’s victory especially significant.

The Rev. Al Sharpton, speaking from the Apollo stage, placed Jackson’s later worldwide success in the context of that Harlem debut.

“Before there was a *Thriller*, before there was a moonwalk, there was the Apollo,” Sharpton said. “And that is where Michael started.”

Sharpton urged the crowd to remember Jackson not only for the controversies that followed him in adulthood but also for breaking racial barriers in the entertainment industry. Jackson’s success on MTV and in arenas around the world opened doors for later generations of Black performers, he said.

Outside, the atmosphere shifted repeatedly between mourning and celebration. Fans cried as they discussed Jackson’s death, then erupted into cheers when familiar bass lines sounded from portable speakers. Groups attempted the moonwalk on the sidewalk, while passing cars played Jackson songs through open windows.

Many in line said they had never met Jackson but felt connected to him through music that had accompanied childhoods, weddings, school dances and family gatherings. Parents brought children who knew Jackson primarily through videos and later recordings. Older fans remembered the Jackson 5’s matching outfits, tightly choreographed routines and string of Motown hits.

Jackson died Thursday, June 25, after suffering cardiac arrest at his rented home in Los Angeles. He was 50. Authorities have not yet announced a final cause of death, and the circumstances surrounding his collapse remain under investigation.

In Harlem, however, the focus Tuesday remained on his music and the beginning of his career.

As evening approached, the line outside the Apollo continued to extend down 125th Street. Theater workers moved mourners through the auditorium in groups, but new arrivals kept coming—turning the blocks around the Apollo into a sprawling, open-air tribute to the boy who first won over its audience more than four decades ago.
